title: Scientists Study How a Queen Mole-Rat's Scent Shapes Colony Life
summary:
Naked mole-rats share work within their colonies. Some members search for food, while others care for the young. The queen has babies. A study found that a chemical scent produced by queens helps keep other colony members from fighting or reproducing.

Gary Lewin, a neuroscientist at the Max Delbrück Center in Berlin, Germany, studies how naked mole-rats use their senses. He previously discovered that they use scent to identify mole-rats from other colonies. That raised another question: do odors also matter within a colony?

Lewin and his team identified isopropyl myristate, a chemical produced only by queens among the mole-rats they studied. It triggered activity in the animals' olfactory cortex, the brain region that processes smells. This gave the researchers a clue that the animals could detect the chemical.

To investigate its effects, the team removed a queen from her colony. They then applied isopropyl myristate to the colony every day for three months. Lewin reported that there was no fighting or mating throughout that period. Mating is part of animal reproduction.

When the researchers stopped adding the odor, the mole-rats began fighting. A few weeks later, mating occurred and a new queen emerged. The experiment showed that the chemical could affect colony behavior even while the queen was absent. The team shared its findings in the journal Nature.

A separate experiment examined reproduction more closely. The researchers separated male and female pairs from the colony. They exposed some pairs to the queen's scent and left others without it. After four weeks, none of the females exposed to the scent had mated. In the group without the scent, five of six females were pregnant.

Blood tests revealed changes in female mole-rats' hormones, chemical signals that influence body functions. Isopropyl myristate lowered progesterone levels and raised prolactin levels. The researchers linked these changes to the prevention of pregnancy.

The team also found that queens produced the chemical only when pregnant or preparing to become pregnant. Together, the experiments help explain how a scent connects a queen's reproductive condition with the behavior and reproduction of other colony members.
why_it_matters: The study helps explain how a chemical signal can connect a queen's reproductive condition with behavior and reproduction elsewhere in her colony.
